MorphoHand · real_v1 · 2026-09-04

UR5e-mounted hand: wrist geometry, grasp preload, and controlled slip to vertical

Every arm result in this program so far stood the UR5e on a 300 mm pedestal, bolted the palm plate straight to the tool flange, and let the arm carry the hand without knowing it was there. Correcting all three: the pedestal buys nothing, the wrist stack is free at every length tested, and 23° of the reorientation's alignment turns out to have been the wrist sagging rather than the hand turning.

What was not in the scene

one flat table, 100 mm of wrist hardware, and a declared payload

The chained task — grasp, lift, reorient, set into a countersink, gait — has run on a UR5e since 2026-09-03 with three assumptions that were never variables. The robot stood on a 300 mm pedestal. The palm plate was bolted straight to the tool flange, because the menagerie UR5e's attachment site is where a gripper goes. And the arm carried the hand without knowing it was there.

None of the three is the bench. The robot is bolted to the same flat table as the work; there is a coupling, a servo bank and its wiring between the flange and the first finger joint, about 100 mm of it; and a real UR5e is told its payload with set_payload, after which its servo loop holds position under a load it is rated to 5 kg for. All three are now parameters of build_real_v1_arm_scene.py (--base, --wrist-stack, --stack-density, --payload-gravcomp). The stack is a 40 mm cylinder at 700 kg/m³, taking the hand from 222 to 574 g.

A bug the change exposed

The arm scene builder copied the design scene's world by whitelist — lights, floor, object. Building an arm scene from a countersink scene therefore dropped the countersink, and the tool stood on a bare plane while the file name said otherwise. It now copies everything except the hand.

The pedestal is free

8 spawn-jittered seeds per cell · 8 gait cycles · no wrist stack

Lowering the mount from 300 mm to the table surface changes nothing measurable. Every height solves the home pose on the same IK branch with the arm's lowest link at +0.163 m — the shoulder — and no link below the table. Across the study the differential IK reports 24 unreachable poses in 1608 rollouts, all at one standing position: 650 mm back and 200 mm across, where 6 of 8 seeds ask for a pose the arm cannot make. The second table can go.

Told its payload, the arm carries the stack for free

tool driven into the 45° seat, published carry grip of 0.3 mm, 500 mm standoff

The wrist stack costs nothing at any length tested. Declaring the payload takes the palm's error at the top of the lift from 0.97 to 0.01 mm, and with that, 0, 50, 100 and 150 mm of stack all complete every seed at 33 deg/cycle, and the tool ends within 2.5° of vertical in every case. Without the declaration the same 150 mm loses the tool on every seed.

The declaration also inverts the grip that works. On the sagging arm the seam needed more commanded interference the longer the wrist got; on the stiff one the published 0.3 mm is already right and more is worse, because the extra closure torques the tool out of the seat on the way down rather than compensating a deflection that is no longer there.

Bench specification

One flat table, no pedestal. Mount at 500 mm, which is where the reach study left it and which now needs no adjustment. Declare the hand's payload to the controller. Carry grip 0.3 mm, as published. Wrist stack anywhere from 0 to 150 mm. Nothing about the hand, the grasp or the gait set-points changes.

What an undeclared payload costs, and where it starts

kept because it is the diagnostic: any wrist that sags behaves this way

The uncompensated sweeps are still the useful characterisation of a compliant wrist, and they collapse onto one number. Stack length, stack mass and standing distance are three independent bench specs, and each moves only palm droop — how far the palm ends up from where it was commanded while holding a load the controller does not model. Droop is deterministic, so it does not inherit the seam's seed-to-seed chaos.

Sweeping the carry grip at each geometry and taking its best cell orders exactly on droop. Every seed completes up to 0.76 mm; 0.97 mm gives 3 of 8 and 1.29 mm gives none. The grip each geometry needs rises with droop over the same range, which is the mechanism: commanded interference minus deflection is the force, so a wrist that deflects more needs a larger command for the same grip.

Where the reorientation's alignment comes from

a new turned seam, taken at the last commanded step of the turn

The turn is an IK sweep of the finger anchor, clipped to ±0.5 rad, followed by a hold with the finger commands frozen. Any alignment gained during that hold is the shaft rolling itself upright inside the grasp. Until now there was no snapshot between the two, so the two contributions were reported as one number.

With them separated, the settle is mostly a correction for the wrist. On an arm that has not been told its payload the turn ends 31.40° off vertical and the hold pulls it back to 12.56°. On the same arm with the payload declared the turn ends 8.03° off vertical, with a spread of 0.42° across spawn jitter, and the hold then makes it worse. Everything in this section is rv05_manual; the next section runs the same measurement on every other hand, and neither number survives.

Can the slip be predicted, controlled and measured?

Predicted: yes, to about a degree, and it degrades with exposure. Tilt at the last commanded turn step is 0.42° sd over spawn jitter; after 150 settling steps the settled tilt has sd 0.14°, after 900 it is 1.63°. The shaft is rolling away from an unstable configuration, so the longer it is allowed to roll the less the seeds agree.

Controlled: by settling time, and only downwards. The best cell is 150 steps (0.3 s) at 6.76°; longer holds drift back out. Gripping through the turn does not work as the other control: extra closure held through the sweep takes the commanded tilt from 8.0° to 39.4° and nothing completes at any of the four non-zero settings.

Measured: already, on the bench, at 0.017° rms. The reorientation turns the shaft about a horizontal axis, so the vane tag stays in the camera's view for the whole sweep and morphohand.bench.tags reports the tool's tilt directly. This is the opposite of the gait, where the shaft spins about the vertical and a single tag leaves view within about 60°.

So on this hand the settle is not needed once the payload is declared. It was worth 23° on a sagging wrist and it is worth nothing on a stiff one, where rv05_manual delivers 8.03° directly and repeatably. The remaining use for the turned seam is as a monitor: it separates a hand that reoriented the tool from a wrist that dropped it into place, and the next section is what that gate is for.

The same turn on ten hands

the published cell, unretuned, on every real_v1 design that has a CEM grasp — 10 designs × 88 rollouts

Every number above was measured on one morphology. Each design was given the identical commanded chain — same turn schedule, same ±0.5 rad budget, same 0.3 mm carry grip, same seat, its own CEM grasp — and the turn was read at the same seam. Of 10 designs, 3 still have the tool in the air with at least two pads on it at the last commanded turn step, 2 finish the chain in at least one seed, and 1 finishes it in every seed.

why the seam needs a contact gate

In 5 of 8 seeds rv04_mid_sp40 reaches that seam with zero pads on the tool and the tool sitting at z = 51 mm, the depth of the countersink. It dropped the shaft during the turn and the shaft landed in its seat, which is vertical by construction, so the seam reads 8.0° of tilt at best and 12.4° on average — a better number than the hand that actually turned it. held_turn, two pads and the tool above 80 mm, is what separates the two.

What does replicate is that closure through the turn is not the control. At every non-zero squeeze, on every hand, nothing completes; on both hands that turn the tool at all, the commanded tilt gets worse rather than better.

One result from the payload sweep does carry across hands, and it is about the grasp rather than the tilt. On an arm that has not been told its payload rv03_narrowy_sp40 holds the tool through the turn in 1 of 8 seeds; declaring it takes that to 8 of 8. rv00_wide_sp40 and rv05_manual hold in both. The sag costs some hands the tool, not just the alignment.

This is a transfer test of one tuned cell, not a design ranking. The turn angle, the axis fraction and the ±0.5 rad budget were all fitted on rv05_manual, and the height of the rotation axis relative to the contacts is the variable that decided whether a real_v1 hand reoriented at all in the 2026-08-28 search. So the table says the 8° is a property of this hand and this fit; it does not say the other nine cannot reorient with a fit of their own. What would settle that is one axis refit per design — --axis-k and the anchor height, the same two knobs the reorient-mechanism study swept — and this table rerun on the refits.

What load it can drive

a Coulomb brake about the tool's own axis, armed once the tool is seated

A countersink is a friction brake, not a thread: it returns μNr and the press sets N through the wedge, so the resisting torque a gaiting hand has ever worked against is whatever the geometry supplied — about 7 mN·m on a flat plane. --screw-torque adds a named one, opposing whatever rotation there is and doing no work when the tool is still.

Raising the commanded grip does not extend that. Crossing torque with --carry-squeeze on one scene, 0.8 mm is worse than 0.3 at every torque including zero, because on a stiff wrist the extra closure is interference rather than compensation.

torque (mN·m)0.3 mm grip deg/cy0.8 mm gripdeg/cy

On the sagging arm the same relay ran flat to 20 mN·m at 1.5 mm of commanded grip. Both cells are the same fingers on the same seat, and they differ in commanded interference, achieved pad force and wrist stiffness at once, so they do not compare as grip settings. What separates them is pad force, which this chain commands open-loop and never measures — the drivable torque cannot be quoted as a number for this hand until it does.

The knob's validity, and its bench equivalent

The tool is 24 g with an axial inertia of 1.9×10-6 kg·m², so a brake much past 20 mN·m can overshoot zero inside a timestep and pump the shaft instead of stopping it. That reads as a turn past the 1.684 gear ceiling and is flagged per rollout; 3 cells trip it here (20 mN·m in the relay arm, 20 mN·m in the release arm), which marks where the range ends. On the bench a cone cannot supply a set torque at all — the only knobs are the press and the seat material. A calibrated one needs a brake under the receptacle: the socket on a short shaft in a bushing with a preloaded friction washer, and the preload screw sets a direction-independent torque a wrench can read.

Next measurements

  1. Refit the turn per design and rerun the ten-hand table. The axis fraction --axis-k, the turn angle and the anchor height were fitted on rv05_manual, so the 10-hand result measures transfer of one fit, not the hands. Sweep those two knobs per design the way docs/experiments/20260828-real_v1_reorient did, then re-read the turned seam. Until that runs, the 8° is a one-hand number and nothing in this page says a second hand can reach it.
  2. Put the contact gate in every tilt report. A tool dropped into a countersink reads vertical, and rv04_mid_sp40 scores better than rv05_manual on tilt alone. held_turn (two pads, tool above 80 mm) is one line in probe_real_v1_chain; the same substitution belongs in the scorecard and in the bench’s AprilTag read, where a seated tool and a held one are equally vertical to the camera.
  3. Cross the thread load with the grip. The drivable torque moved from 4–12 to 20 mN·m when the commanded grip went 0.3 → 1.5 mm, but those two cells also differ in wrist stiffness. Run --screw-torque × --carry-squeeze on one scene and report torque per millimetre of commanded interference; that is the number a fastener spec would be checked against.
  4. Close the grip loop. Pad force is commanded minus achieved, the finger servos calibrate to one spring constant across the hand, and position is readable at the control rate. Estimate force from deflection and trim --carry-squeeze to hold a target rather than searching for an open-loop value that depends on the robot. This is the only item above that removes a whole class of sweep.
  5. Run the relay's Cartesian legs through the gates. scripts/real_v1_trajectory_clearance.py and the servo-limit check, then export a plan. It is a new path shape, and three of the four plans that have reached the control station failed exactly that check.
  6. Build the tag collar for the gait. Three AprilTags at 120° on a 60 mm printed collar above the pad ring, so the one camera reads the spin through a full turn instead of the ±60° a single tag covers. morphohand.bench.tags already carries the geometry for a vane; the collar is the same maths with an ID lookup and an unwrap.
  7. Instrument the axial slip. The floor-free relay holds the tool for every cycle and lowers it 11 mm per cycle; slip_mm_per_cycle reports it and no reward term, scorecard entry or design metric on either topology does. Add it to the scorecard before attempting a persistent-grasp gait.
